cells.tense: The repetitions belong to you and they don't take you away from people — you're at the table and still working at the thing.
cells.ask: Next time the work pulls you in, tell one person near you what you're making. No preamble. See whether saying it gives something back.
cells.core:
The refining isn't eating you and it isn't walling you off. Time alone is where the work happens, and you come back from it still able to sit with people — the two feed each other instead of fighting. That's the shape this holds right now.

So there's room to find out what more it can carry. Pick the next thing you'd normally keep to yourself — a half-finished piece, a small discovery, a version that isn't ready. Name it to someone once, just to hear it leave your mouth. Not for feedback and not to teach. Just to see which repetitions are worth keeping.
cells.sheetLine: The work doesn't cost you the room, and it's yours.
cells.verb: keep at the small unglamorous repetitions that build a thing into the body

cells.tense: You're already braced for the version where it's finally good enough — and you're spending today trying to reach it early.
cells.ask: Pick the practice you care most about and set it down for one day. Not as punishment — as a test. Watch what stays when you're not at it.
cells.core:
Somewhere ahead of you is a finish line where it'll finally feel done, and you're burning energy trying to arrive there ahead of time. That's the tell — not laziness, the opposite. The refining has tipped into checking and rechecking, and people start to feel like interruptions instead of company.

What's waiting on the other side is lighter: finishing something and letting it be finished, walking back over to the humans without having the answer first. When you set the thing down and nothing collapses, you'll find out how much of the doing was the work and how much was just staying near it. Step back for a day. What's yours will still be there.

cells.tense: Sitting down to the small repetitions feels like a risk, and you've been keeping your distance from them.
cells.ask: At whatever table you're sitting at now, do one small thing you've been skipping. One sitting, one page, one round. Nothing rides on it.
cells.core:
The practice is right there and you don't pick it up. Not out of laziness — out of a habit that's older than the situation. What's absent isn't ability; it's the plain permission to do the unglamorous thing anyway and not worry about whether it's any good.

What's waiting on the other side isn't a performance. It's a version where the repetitions make you more available to people instead of taking you away from them — the practice gives you something to bring back, not a place to hide. Start small enough that it can't mean anything yet. One page, one round, one sitting. That's enough to learn which door you're standing at.
cells.sheetLine: The steady work isn't dangerous anymore, and you're still treating it like it is.

cells.tense: You're already doing the repetitions — quietly, in the middle of everything else — and calling it something that isn't you doing them.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're better at now than a year ago and say out loud, once, 'I did that.' Not the story. Just the admission.
cells.core:
You've been refining something steady enough that you can do it without thinking, and you talk about it like it happened on its own, or like it's just the work being the work. The repetition is real. You being the one who did it isn't something you've said. That gap is where the room gets a little cold, because people can't quite reach the part of you that's been showing up.

What sits under the modesty isn't modesty — it's a refusal to be the one in the room who did it. Say you did it. That's the whole move. It isn't about credit. It's about letting the person across from you meet the version that practiced, instead of the version that just happens to be good at this.
